title: Maha Shivaratri: the great night of Shiva
hook: a night kept awake, water poured over the lingam, Om Namah Shivaya until dawn
tomorrow: Raksha Bandhan: the thread of protection

segments.voice: Yesterday: Holi, a bonfire for Prahlad and a morning of color. Your line was everyone's the same color today. Did you treat someone as exactly level with you? Today, a night nobody sleeps. Day six hundred seventy-five.

A hunter goes into the forest and finds nothing. All day, nothing. Night falls, and he's too far from home and too stubborn to go back empty-handed. So he climbs a tree beside a pool, where animals will come to drink, and he waits. He hasn't eaten. He can't let himself sleep, or he'll fall. To keep busy, he plucks leaves off the branch, one by one, and drops them. He doesn't look where they land. This is one of the stories told on Maha Shivaratri, and it's about a man who keeps the festival perfectly without knowing it exists.
screen: `A HUNTER WITH NOTHING.` → `A TREE BESIDE A POOL.` → `LEAVES DROPPED IN THE DARK.`

segments.voice: Shiva-ratri: the night of Shiva. Maha: great. It falls on the fourteenth night of the waning moon, in late winter, the last dark before the new moon. The tree the hunter climbed was a bilva tree, whose three-part leaves are sacred to Shiva. And under it, hidden in the dark, was a lingam, the simple rounded stone that stands for Shiva in temples and shrines. All night, his dropped leaves fell on it. Drops from his water pot spilled on it. He fasted, because he had no food. He stayed awake, because he had to. Without meaning to, he had done what Shivaratri asks: fast, keep vigil, offer water and bilva leaves to the lingam. In the Shiva Purana's telling, deer come to the pool through the night, and each one asks to be spared long enough to go home first, and the hunter, softening, lets them go. By dawn, the story says, his heart is changed, and Shiva's grace reaches him. That's what people across India do on this night, on purpose. Temples stay open until morning. Devotees pour water, milk, honey over the lingam, in a rite called abhisheka. Many repeat five syllables, na-mah shi-va-ya, Om Namah Shivaya, bowing to Shiva, over and over until the sky gets light. Different stories are given for the night: Shiva's marriage to Parvati, or the night he drank the world's poison. But the practice is the same: don't sleep through the night that matters.
screen: `MAHA SHIVARATRI: THE GREAT NIGHT.` · `BILVA LEAVES FALL ON A HIDDEN LINGAM.` · `A FAST AND A VIGIL, BY ACCIDENT.` · `OM NAMAH SHIVAYA UNTIL DAWN.` · then, large: `STAY AWAKE FOR WHAT MATTERS.`

segments.voice: Sit upright, the way the hunter had to stay upright on his branch. Follow your breath in and out. When you feel the first urge to stop, to check your phone, to shift, to be done, stay for three more breaths. Just three. Count them gently. Then notice what's here on the other side of that urge. Keep going with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Shivaratri. The night of Shiva, kept awake with fasting, water and bilva leaves on the lingam, and Om Namah Shivaya until dawn.
Your line: stay awake for what matters. Today, give one thing you'd normally half-attend, a conversation, a meal, a walk, your full waking attention. Day six hundred seventy-five.

howItsDone: On Maha Shivaratri many Hindus fast, visit Shiva temples, pour water or milk over the lingam with bilva leaves, and keep vigil through the night repeating Om Namah Shivaya; many temples stay open until dawn.

fork.setup: you're the hunter, hungry after a day with nothing. a deer comes to the pool and asks to go home first, promising to return. what do you do?
options: climb down and chase her off.
fork.reveal: in the Shiva Purana's telling he lets the deer go, softening through the night, and by dawn Shiva's grace reaches him.

original.note: Sanskrit: om, namaḥ (bowing to), śivāya (to Shiva). na-maḥ-śi-vā-ya is the five-syllable mantra.

trapdoor: what you thought: Shivaratri is a night of prayer for very devout people.
what it means: fasting, vigil and simple offerings on the lingam, which even a hungry hunter could do by accident.
what a scholar hears: the hunter story is told in the Shiva Purana; Om Namah Shivaya, the five-syllable mantra, appears in the Shri Rudram of the Yajurveda as namaḥ śivāya.

sources.ref: Shiva Purana, Koti Rudra Samhita (the hunter and the bilva tree on Shivaratri)
Krishna Yajurveda, Taittiriya Samhita 4.5 (Shri Rudram: namah shivaya)

notes: Confirm the Shiva Purana location of the hunter story and the deer who ask to go home first; tellings vary (the hunter is sometimes named).
Shivaratri date: Krishna Chaturdashi of Phalguna (purnimanta) / Magha (amanta). The script says 'the fourteenth night of the waning moon, in late winter'.
Confirm Shri Rudram as the textual home of 'namah shivaya' (Taittiriya Samhita 4.5.8).
The poison story (Neelakantha) is mentioned briefly and left for a later Shivaratri day.
